speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: asked	the Minister for Defence (a) in the past three years, from which countries did most of the cyberattacks on the Ministry's military data systems originate; (b) how long did it take the Ministry to detect the breach of its system in the February 2017 attack; and (c) what steps have been taken to strengthen the Ministry's IT systems.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: asked the Minister for Defence (a) if he can provide an update on the Ministry's investigations into the cyberattack on its IT system that took place in February 2017; (b) whether the perpetrators have been uncovered; and (c) what steps may be taken to prevent or minimise the risk from such attacks in future.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because computer systems are designed to facilitate connectivity, they are inherently vulnerable to cyberattackers from any location motivated by mischief, criminal theft or national interest, at varying levels of sophistication.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Symantec, a global cybersecurity company, recently reported more than 430 million new pieces of malware in just one year.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) systems are no different and, on a daily level, experience hundreds of thousands of cyber intrusion attempts ranging from simple probes to sophisticated cyber espionage efforts.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The latter include covert attacks by highly-skilled operators who mask or obfuscate their actions by routing through multiple countries to hide their real point of origin.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: MINDEF/SAF adopts a multi-layered, risk-based approach to cyber defence, which balances between connectivity and speed on one hand, and security on the other.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On one extreme are networks which contain sensitive military information, which are physically separated from the Internet and further protected with encryption and access controls.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On the other extreme are systems, like I-net, aimed to facilitate connectivity and ease of use with limited security features which require some personal information of users for access.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The I-net system contains no classified information and is designed to allow National Service (NS)men on In-Camp Training to access the Internet for civilian work and personal matters when in camp.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: However, across all MINDEF/SAF networks, multiple sensors, intrusion detection systems and firewalls are placed at critical nodes to detect intrusion attempts and activities.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Computer systems globally are updated consistently with new applications.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It takes about 120 days, on average, for industry players to develop a patch.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Cyberattackers exploit this window of vulnerability by evading the most commonly used commercial sensors and anti-virus signatures.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Industry reports cite an average of about 150 days, five months, before a breach is discovered in any computer system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For example, the hacking into the US Government's Office of Personnel Management began in November 2013 but was only discovered in March 2014.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: This breach resulted in the loss of up to 18 million personal data records.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More recently, hackers breached the email servers of the Democratic National Committee in mid-2015 and this was detected only in April 2016, almost a year later and, by which time, all of their emails and chats had been stolen.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The modus operandi was consistent with a covert attack, with means used to mask the perpetrator's actions and intent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Our investigations are ongoing but findings will be kept confidential for security reasons.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We will also review the storage of personal data on our Internet systems to minimise risks of cybertheft.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Are we investigating and prosecuting some of them?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With these intrusions, how many of these investigations lead to successful prosecution of the perpetrators?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If the perpetrators can be identified and are locally situated, we will make sure that we take them through the process of law.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Having said that, prosecution and punishment are just one way.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have to do a lot of other things.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Technologically, as I have mentioned, various sensors can be put at critical nodes which will help us detect such intrusions.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The system architecture is important, which is why MINDEF had separated the I-net system from the more confidential systems.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In this case, the perpetrator went through the window but could not access the house because the house is separated.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: More importantly, the weakest link is often the human factor.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A lot more education is needed because we can have the most sophisticated cyber defence system, but if we do not have the discipline and we plug an external device into our office network, it can be infected.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: All these are things that we would have to do.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, have the perpetrators who were responsible for the recent attack on MINDEF been identified?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, will the hackers be able to make use of the personal information that they have obtained from the recent attack for future hacking or other cybercrimes?
